items.title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
items.content: Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification , Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers : “ Hunger beats tenure” This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. Enough said. His advice for juniors Pick business impact over backlog : In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea : Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! Build it over a weekend : I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype. Focus on one good idea : In my experience, junior people often make the mistake of cramming multiple ideas into a single prototype , hiding three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones. Lean into your fresh perspective : If you’re working on something user-facing, you have a unique amount of empathy for users and thus a much better sense for how the product works or doesn’t work for them. Well said, Felix! Get web search results as clean, structured Markdown, using roughly 50% fewer tokens than JSON on average. Easily integrate Markdown search results into your AI workflows across 100+ SerpApi APIs! swyx’s commentary: we’re proud to work with AI native sponsors that you can use in your engineering workflows! Check out the token savings of Markdown - from 361k tokens to 38k for Google properties! AI Twitter Recap Genie 4: DeepMind's Real-Time World Model Adds Audio, Physics and Gemini Planning Launch : Google DeepMind introduced Genie 4, its "most realistic and interactive world model yet." Users can explore generated environments in real time and steer events, camera angles and actions with text ( GDM , Sundar Pichai , Demis Hassabis ). Architecture : The model is built on Gemini Omni. Gemini runs in the loop to plan multi-step events and keep scenes coherent ( features , Eli Collins ). Native audio : It generates ambient sound, music and real-time dialogue with characters, a first for Genie ( Shlomi Fruchter ). Physics and photorealism : DeepMind claims aerodynamics, collisions and natural human motion. Genie 3's worlds were "too static," and Genie 4 responds to prompted events mid-generation ( Fruchter ). Robotics angle : DeepMind positions Genie 4 as a step toward safe virtual environments for testing agents and robots. Demos : Gemini 3.8 Flash decomposes tasks, checks each step and replans as the scene changes. A Gemini 4 Argon + Genie 4 experiment simulates an Apollo humanoid playing checkers ( summary ). Availability : The research preview is open to trusted testers now. Google AI Ultra subscribers will get access next via Project Genie, followed by early-access partners through the Gemini API and AI Studio, which marks Genie's first API availability ( Logan Kilpatrick , waitlist ). Early-access impressions : Users with early access describe prompting a "neogothic brutalist city," then adding dragons and an NPC live. They call it "not flawless" but a large leap over Genie 3 ( Ethan Mollick , venturetwins , Riley Goodside ). AI for Math and Science: CFSG Formalized, ETH Disproof Claims Axiom formalizes CFSG : Axiom announced a complete Lean auto-formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups. The original proof spans about 15,000 pages across roughly 500 papers by more than 100 mathematicians ( Axiom , Kevin Weil ). Process : An agent swarm produced about 50M lines of Lean in 24 days. Agents claimed tasks, reviewed each other's work and merged through GitHub, with human guidance, and reportedly fixed hundreds of errata in the published proof ( omarsar0 , kimmonismus ). Context : Researchers note it displaces the four-color theorem as the largest computer-verified proof. Few humans understand the full CFSG proof ( hyhieu226 , Stella Biderman ). Exponential Time Hypothesis : OpenAI announced new results in harmonic analysis, complexity theory and QFT, including a claimed refutation of ETH, with materials in its openai/math repo ( Romain Huet , Dan ). Anthropic's parallel claim : Anthropic reportedly says Claude independently disproved ETH, finding the key algorithm on Oct 16 with "14M output tokens and no human input." PSI also claims progress on five open quantum physics problems with computer-checked proofs ( Rundown roundup ). Physics follow-up : A Yang-Mills Working Group published a statement interpreting an AI result related to the existence of quantum Yang-Mills theory ( KITP ). Smaller results : Ten Claude agents proved in Lean that seven electrons on a sphere settle into a pentagonal bipyramid, a case of the Thomson problem ( Vals ). Separately, a Stanford study had 29 experts rate AI-proposed research problems and judged about one-third "interesting" ( Percy Liang ). Independent Evals: AA Index v5, FrontierCode 2.0 and GPT-6.1 Terra Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 : 60% of the index now comes from private or held-out sets ( announcement ). Composition : It adds FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench-Science, swaps HLE for HLE-Diamond, and drops GDPval-AA, SciCode and AA-LCR. Four categories carry equal 25% weights ( weights ). items.title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
items.content: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. A model launch is also an API launch Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own products do not cover. As we have said for 4 straight years now on the podcast , having good evals is golden. The brain and the hands Our favorite mental model in the episode is the distinction between an agent's brain and its hands. In Managed Agents , Anthropic separates the session log and harness from the sandbox that executes code. The harness can persist while an execution environment is created when needed; a failed sandbox does not have to take the whole agent session with it. We covered this in the Thariq pod : Claude Code’s Next Era — Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic — Latent Space Shipping Opus/Sonnet 5.5, Mods, Plugins, Projects, Tag while Pacing the Frontier Latent Space The same separation gives security a useful architectural property. If generated code runs in a sandbox that never receives a service credential, there is no credential in that sandbox for the code to read. The episode describes credentials held separately and attached through a proxy, alongside controls on where sandbox traffic can go. Anthropic's containment write-up describes the wider set of isolation and network controls used across its products. The distinction matters for performance too. The guests say an earlier approach put the whole coding agent in a sandbox behind an API. Starting the environment and agent added work before the first response; if the sandbox disappeared, so did the running agent. Separating the pieces allowed the platform to pursue lower latency and better reliability while keeping execution isolated. It is a helpful lens for anyone designing an agent runtime. Ask which parts need to survive, which parts execute untrusted work, and which secrets actually need to be present where code runs. The implementation will differ between products, but those questions remain useful. An agent that helps another agent remember Managed Agents also provides a base for experiments in memory and multi-agent workflows. Dreaming is simply implemented as one agent inspecting another agent's prior work and writing memories back. That makes the feature an example of building a higher-level behavior out of the same underlying managed-agent primitives. Their account of the roadmap is more nuanced than a list of features. Memory and learning remain important, but the team says more of its immediate attention has moved to safety as model launches have become harder. They also discuss keeping the base harness relatively simple, while letting developers experiment with verifiers, parallel agents and other strategies on top. Ideas mentioned for future platform capabilities should be treated as plans, not shipped promises. The conversation about evaluations follows naturally. A harness is an application, but improving one starts to resemble research: pick a goal, measure behavior, inspect failures, and iterate. The guests and hosts discuss using models to help build and analyze evaluations, while retaining enough judgment to decide whether the evaluation reflects a real user's job. Show notes Claude Opus 5.5 announcement — Anthropic's launch notes on model behavior, evaluation and pricing. Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang at Anthropic's partner summit — Anthropic identifies their platform engineering and product roles. Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands — The session, harness and sandbox architecture discussed in the episode. How Anthropic contains Claude across products — How Anthropic describes isolation, credentials and network controls across its products. Effective harnesses for long-running agents — Earlier Anthropic work on the challenge of maintaining progress across context windows. Anthropic model system cards — The company's public model evaluation and safety documentation. Anthropic S-1 breakdown — The numbers and context behind the newly recorded introduction. Coding From the Himalayas With an Offline AI Agent
items.content: When we talk about working remotely , we take a lot of things for granted, especially reliable internet and power. But sometimes, working remotely means trying to get something done on a flight, during a long train ride, or somewhere with little or no network. I moved to the foothills of the Himalayas a year ago. I love the peace of living here, but it also comes with its own challenges, including network and power outages . Things I didn’t think about as much before are now part of planning my work. I work as a Principal Engineer at Thomson Reuters , where I spend most of my time coding and reviewing my teammates’ code. Coding agents are already a big part of my everyday workflow, which made me curious about how much of that workflow I could keep using offline. Working from the foothills of the Himalayas. Photo of my workspace. If you’re someone like me, who enjoys working with technology but also finds peace in quiet, remote places where the network doesn’t always cooperate, this article is for you. It’s also for anyone who has wondered whether a coding agent can run entirely on their laptop, with the internet switched off. I tried running a coding agent locally on my laptop to see how much work I could actually get done offline. What can we do offline? A project already on your laptop gives us plenty to work with. We can ask an agent to explain an unfamiliar function, investigate a failing test, refactor a small piece of code, or help finish a feature. These tasks can run offline when the model, project dependencies and test tools are available locally. Downloading a new package or looking something up on the web will still need a connection. Where OpenCode fits OpenCode is an open-source coding agent that works with your project. You give it a task, and it can read files, propose edits and run commands such as the test suite. In our setup, its permission prompts let us review commands and changes before allowing them. I picked OpenCode because it lets me keep that workflow in the terminal while connecting to a model running on my own laptop. Ollama handles running the model; OpenCode handles the interaction with the project. OpenCode on my Mac, with Qwen3.5 9B selected as the local model. Open-weight models, including Qwen , make this possible: their weights, the learned parameters used to generate responses, can be downloaded and run locally. With Ollama running Qwen on the same laptop, OpenCode can send its requests to a local service. We download everything first, then disconnect the internet for the coding task. Aider is another option if you prefer a guided editing workflow; it also supports Ollama. We are using OpenCode throughout this walkthrough so that the setup and results stay consistent. OpenCode works with the project files and sends model requests to Ollama on the same laptop. Ollama runs Qwen locally. Choosing an open-source model Qwen comes in different sizes. I wanted a model we could run locally that could also use an agent’s tools. For context, here are published results for two Qwen sizes and another open-weight option, as reported in Qwen’s model card . LiveCodeBench v6 tests code generation on programming problems. BFCL-V4 evaluates function calling, which matters when a model needs to choose a tool and give it the right arguments. Higher scores are better on both. Model LiveCodeBench v6 BFCL-V4 Qwen3.5 4B 55.8 50.3 Qwen3.5 9B (used here) 65.6 66.1 gpt-oss-20b 74.6 Not reported The above table scores reported in Qwen’s model card , not measurements from this laptop. “Not reported” means the source does not provide that score. We’re using Qwen3.5 9B for this walkthrough. Its stronger published coding and tool-calling results than the 4B variant made it a useful starting point. The table doesn’t measure laptop speed or the whole OpenCode workflow; our offline file edits and tests are the check for that. Model size and memory Model Approx. download Qwen3.5 4B 3.3–4.0 GB Qwen3.5 9B (used here) 6.6–7.6 GB Qwen3.5 27B 17–20 GB Ollama lists all available sizes ; downloads vary by runtime format. Download size isn’t a RAM requirement. Voltti budgets 12–16 GB of memory for a 6.6 GB Qwen3.5 9B build. Our 64k-token OpenCode configuration may need more, so leave room for context and other apps. How OpenCode performed in benchmarks OpenCode has also been tested beyond small demos. The research preprint The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents compared OpenCode, Goose and OpenHands-SDK on 50 Terminal-Bench Pro tasks using two cloud models. Here are the pass rates reported in Table 2. Coding agent Qwen3.6 Plus MiniMax M2.5 Goose 48% [34–62%] 38% [24–52%] OpenCode 50% [36–64%] 46% [32–60%] OpenHands-SDK 50% [36–64%] 46% [32–60%] The brackets show 95% confidence intervals. The authors caution that most differences in pass rate were not statistically clear. The study also reported substantially higher token use for OpenCode : about 40 times Goose’s tokens per solved task. These runs used cloud APIs and different models from ours, so they do not predict how local Qwen3.5 9B will perform. Initial setup While you still have access to the internet, follow the complete setup in the GitHub README . It covers installing the tools, downloading the project, and installing OpenCode 1.19.4 . The project includes the examples, tests and configuration for using Qwen locally. Once that is ready, keep Terminal A open in the project folder. Before starting, it helps to know what opencode.json does . This is OpenCode’s project configuration . In our file, model and small_model both select Qwen3.5 9B, and baseURL points to Ollama at http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1. Only the local provider is enabled. It also asks before editing files or running shell commands, and blocks the web tools. The full configuration is in the repository. We still disconnect the network for the offline test. items.title: [AINews] Anthropic files for $2T IPO in 2 weeks: 1400% growth rate, 48% of revenue through cloud partners, 85% margin, $1B op profit in Q2, $134B cash in bank and $10B lifetime burn
items.content: Today is one of those days that is tougher to cover for a normally-engineer audience that isn’t used to reading most S-1’s, let alone 350 pages of one of the most unusual S-1’s of all time : Better visualized: With significant operating leverage causing the first profitable quarter in Anthropic history (adjusted for $1B/quarter of SBC): The incredible efficiency story is told in two loops, and of course you know, we love loop: The pitch going forward is “virtual collaborators” (don’t say agent!) for over a billion knowledge workers by 2028: We believe we have reached an inflection point where AI systems can function as genuine collaborators in professional work. They quickly complete substantive tasks that might otherwise occupy a skilled professional for several hours, a full day, or longer. AI systems are also becoming increasingly capable of performing tasks that were previously too difficult or costly to complete or surfacing original insights and analyses. We refer to these AI systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels as Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators carry the access rights, system connections, and context that their organizations grant them , which allows them to function more accurately and reliably. They can navigate and use internal tools and execute workflows that span multiple steps that require sustained reasoning. Virtual Collaborators are AI designed to be embedded where work gets done, and our aim is to continue extending them to knowledge workers globally, a population that is estimated to exceed one billion in 2028. And we end with a useful map of all of Anthropic’s offerings on one screen: AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Anthropic files its S-1. Reactions and highlights What happened Anthropic publicly filed its S-1 on Monday at ~9am ET. It plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT," and the filing shows a company that has crossed into operating profitability while carrying enormous compute commitments. Lead-up. Timing was reported by The Information ( @kimmonismus ), Fox Business ( @negligible_cap ) and Bloomberg ( @kimmonismus ). The IPO itself had been expected around Nov 9 ( @kimmonismus ). Official filing. Anthropic announced the filing with the standard registration disclaimer ( @AnthropicAI ). The EDGAR link was posted by @rishdotblog , and the ticker was flagged by @kimmonismus . Revenue. Revenue went from $41M in 2023 to $16.3B in H1 2026, roughly 14x year over year. Q2 alone was $11.6B, up 1,368% YoY ( @futurenomics , @kimmonismus ). Profitability. Q2 operating profit was $974M. H1 operating cash flow was +$3.9B. The headline $80.7B H1 net loss includes $81.1B of non-cash charges tied to financial instruments ( @kimmonismus ). Capital efficiency. Anthropic has raised $141.1B in aggregate. It holds $112.4B in cash plus $19.3B in short-term investments. Implied lifetime burn is about $9.7B ( @SemiAnalysis_ ), which SemiAnalysis called "likely the most efficient scaling of a business in the history of capitalism." Compute commitments. Non-cancelable commitments run deep into the next decade ( @scaling01 ). They include up to $120.5B for NVIDIA-powered compute through SpaceXAI, under agreements extending into 2029 ( @kimmonismus ). Pre-training delay. Anthropic disclosed it recently delayed pre-training of a new frontier model ( @scaling01 ). Anchor investor. Altimeter said it will participate "majorly" in the IPO on top of its existing stake ( @altcap ). Key numbers (facts from the filing vs. derived estimates) Gross margin trajectory ( @jaminball ): 2023: 37% 2024: −95% 2025: 40% H1 2025: 12% H1 2026: 85% Jamin Ball's summary of the filing ( @jaminball ): Revenue growth above 1,000% YoY in the last quarter. 21% free-cash-flow margin over the last six months. Less than $10B burned in total to reach more than $16B in quarterly revenue. He also cited a $16.8B Q3 figure that has been widely reported but is not in the S-1 ( @jaminball ). Cash and burn figures don't agree across accounts. SemiAnalysis puts burn at $9.7B; Austen Allred puts it at $9.4B. Cash is quoted as ~$132B (futurenomics) or $134B "today" (Ball). Austen claims $6.7B of positive cumulative FCF from 2023 to June 2026 and $575M/month of current FCF ( @Austen ). That sits awkwardly next to a $9.4B lifetime burn, so treat derived cash-flow figures with caution. How the $141B raise breaks down ( @jaminball ): About $128.6B of preferred stock proceeds. $11.3B of convertible notes from Amazon and Google issued in 2023–2025. About $5B has converted. The remaining $6.2B of principal carries a $108.6B fair-value liability, because it converts at $2–5/share versus a ~$59 Series H price. The convertibles are effectively ~1.8B shares, not debt, and that mark-to-market drives most of the GAAP loss. Remaining pieces: ~$0.6B of SAFEs/common and ~$0.7B from pre-2023 rounds. Distribution through cloud marketplaces ( @Bensign , @saranormous ): 48% of H1 2026 revenue (about $7.8B) flowed through Bedrock, Vertex and Azure Marketplace, up from 11% in 2023. Marketplace fees sit in sales, marketing and partnerships, not cost of revenue. They therefore never touch the headline 85% gross margin. Channel-partner fees rose about $2.7B YoY. Bensign's read: hyperscalers get paid twice, once for the compute and again for distribution. Compute efficiency. Aymeric Roucher derives $2.08 of revenue per $1 of compute, which implies under one year of payback on compute ( @AymericRoucher ). Internal use of Claude ( @TheRundownAI ): Internal Claude usage passed monthly personnel costs (excluding stock pay) in April. Measured at list prices, that usage grew more than 250x between January and September 2026. Separately, State of AI data says Claude "led" 27% of Anthropic's R&D ( @thursdai_pod ). Lockup. It is a staggered drip lasting more than a year, not the usual 180-day cliff. Some holders can sell on day one, which should smooth float ( @saranormous ). Public Benefit Fu

items.content: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. Here are the pelicans for the different reasoning levels. This pelican for "max" cost 11.3161 cents and took 4 minutes and 11 seconds: Here's a new comparison grid showing pelicans for every reasoning level of OpenAI's current frontier lineup: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna. GPT-6.1 Terra is priced at $1/million input tokens and $5/million output - almost half the price of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and around 10x the price of GPT-6 Luna. items.title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
items.content: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) Tags: browsers , go , javascript , jeff-lindsay , shot-scraper

items.content: 2 months ago we covered Z.ai CEO Prof Jie Tang’s prediction that we’d get a Fable-class open weights model by year end . 2 weeks ago Meta achieved a Fable-class model in closed source , but, with 2.5 months left to go, we finally got it - a 2.8T open weights model beating Fable 5.1, not just Fable 5, at that: View post on X ↗ with even better efficiency: View post on X ↗ You can tell Kimi is proud of their latest model by how fancy their landing page is: As usual we don’t get much research detail - the update is somewhat similar to Z.ai ’s 5.2-5.3 bump - a minor version bump for a lot more post-training: Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. AI News for 10/22/2026-10/23/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Kimi K3.1 Pro launch and reactions What happened Moonshot launched Kimi K3.1 Pro with near-frontier independent benchmark results, a substantial increase in model size, and an open-weight release promised for November 4, 2026. The model: Moonshot describes K3.1 Pro as a multimodal, “3T-class” mixture-of-experts model with 2.8 trillion total parameters, 104 billion active parameters, and a 1-million-token context window . Its advertised strengths include full-project coding, Blender/CAD work, financial modeling, and long-running agents. @Kimi_Moonshot Availability: Standard and Highspeed versions launched across Kimi’s website/app, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and API. Moonshot claims Highspeed preserves intelligence while generating output 2–3× faster ; the official-account summary says it costs twice as much . The launch also includes Kimi Hosted Agents , a managed harness with a 24/7 execution environment for long-running work and multi-agent collaboration. @ZhihuFrontier , @ZhihuFrontier Independent general-capability result: Artificial Analysis placed K3.1 Pro fourth on its Intelligence Index, scoring 55 , behind Opus 5.5 at 58 and Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full at 56. Its strongest improvements were agentic rather than uniformly distributed across knowledge and science tests. @ArtificialAnlys Independent coding result: Arena placed it #8 in Code Arena: WebDev, at 1,692 points , up nine places and 37 points over Kimi K3. Moonshot returned to Arena’s top four labs . @arena Independent cyber result: Despite deliberately reducing cyber-related training, it subsequently scored 64% on Artificial Analysis’ Cyber Index —the highest publicly accessible result and second overall, behind trusted-access GPT-6 Sol Daybreak Blue at 69%. @ArtificialAnlys The reaction split: Enthusiasm about a prospective open-weight frontier contender was followed by concerns about inference economics, weaker results on some interactive tasks, benchmark presentation, and allegations of undisclosed paid promotion. These are distinct issues: benchmark quality does not establish deployment economics, and promotional misconduct allegations do not establish model capability. @simonw , @maxbittker , @kimmonismus Release status, architecture, and what “open” means here At launch, the API was available; the weights were not . Moonshot’s announcement promises weights by November 4, 2026 . The supplied tweets do not establish the eventual license, redistribution conditions, commercial-use restrictions, checkpoint precision, or complete inference requirements. Consequently, “soon-to-be open-weight” is more precise than the “OSS” or “open source” language used in several reactions. Artificial Analysis explicitly recorded the weights as unpublished. @Kimi_Moonshot , @ArtificialAnlys The release sequence generated confusion: Early reports predicted a release “today” and potentially the strongest open-weight model, explicitly on rumors/leaks ; a follow-up reiterated positive hearsay. Neither was an evaluation. @kimmonismus , @kimmonismus Teasers triggered speculation about November 5 , including whether Moonshot would monetize website access before publishing weights. The official announcement subsequently specified November 4 . @scaling01 , @scaling01 , @bigeagle_xd Initial users reported availability on kimi.com before kimi.ai ; another later reported obtaining access. These are rollout observations, not evidence of a lasting regional restriction. @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex Repeated complaints about suspense and guesses about a symbolic launch time reflected the launch atmosphere, not confirmed scheduling information. @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex Architecturally, 104B active parameters do not make this equivalent to storing a 104B dense model : deployment must accommodate the much larger expert pool, plus runtime state. As an illustrative calculation—not a measured configuration—2.8T parameters alone imply approximately 5.6 TB at 16-bit or 1.4 TB at 4-bit , before quantization metadata and serving overhead. The supplied posts disclose no layer layout, expert routing configuration, attention design, training-compute budget, or measured full-context serving footprint. That matters for the “local model” narrative. One enthusiastic post called it Fable 5.1 intelligence available locally, then corrected that weights would arrive November 4. Separately, @giffmana warned against calling trillion-parameter models “local” when deployment requires substantial accelerator infrastructure. Self-hostable and consumer-device-local are different properties

items.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
items.content: In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture . Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem , then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem , and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis . The models are suddenly good at math. The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Problem complexity Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity 1 (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity 2 modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts: Look for a counterexample. Take the best known construction and generalize it. Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm. Gowers’ proposed formula for complexity is 2^k + t, where k is the length of the shortest hint sequence and t is the work required to develop it. It is the sort of formula that looks rigorous right up until you try to put a number into it, which is more or less the point. Complexity grows exponentially with the number of insights you need to solve a problem. Most problem solving is the work between these insights. You have a eureka moment, then spend months developing the hint until another conceptual jump becomes possible. For an expert, time spent is a useful proxy for this work, hence t. Hand someone the first unit-distance hint and they still have to do enough work to reach the generalized construction. Useful, but post hoc. You can’t look at the problem and predict it would need x number of hints. So, a problem’s age, the number of tries, and the prize attached to it are common proxies to ascribe difficulty. Characteristics of a given hint A typical insight changes the formulation of the problem. The representation and understanding of the problem change . Two things decide how much a hint is worth: How unlikely it looked before, against how obvious it looks after supplying the hint → This is harder than people realize. In unit distance, many experts did not consider the counterexample as likely. Where it belongs in the sequence: hints are ordered. A third hint is useful only after the work on the first two have made enough progress for it to be actionable. This defeats the naive brute force idea of listing a thousand mathematical techniques and trying every combination 3 . Hints sequence traverses a tree. Initial insights change the problem and reveal the choices that follow. Humans solve problems breadth first Combine k and t and you get the human search pattern . Generate candidate directions, explore them shallowly, abandon most, and commit to a few. A promising direction is abandoned if it does not give enough encouragement early 4 . This is a human constraint: Developing an idea can take months. Before committing, a researcher needs reasons to believe it will lead somewhere: conceptual promise, early results, or experience with similar problems. The longer it takes to find out, the higher the bar for trying the idea. Most research software exists to shrink this time by automating the tedious, mechanical, repeatable work. AI shrinks it far enough that the search pattern itself flips, and everything downstream follows from that. AI and complexity First, t. The model’s equivalent of effort is compute and tokens, spent on one trajectory (test time compute) or spread across parallel agents (parallel test time compute). Pretraining also supplies knowledge that a human researcher would have to locate or reconstruct. No individual expert is aware of every previous development, so occasionally they end up redoing things already done. The bigger difference is how models search: LLMs are depth first Give the model a single prompt and it will give you a solution. Maybe correct, perhaps not. Ask for a proof and it will give you something that approaches a good proof. CoT for these models runs in a greedy depth first manner too. And the process scales. Give parallel agents ten approaches and you get ten attempts developed toward a conclusion. Maybe all distinct, or some overlapping. Each either hits a roadblock or produces an argument that looks right. Left alone, this gets you beautiful false proofs. This seems like a waste of compute and resources, until you add an automated verifier 5 that can prune the completed trajectories and identify the correct ones. With this checker, it is now rational to spend enormous compute on uncertain ideas. You find out whether a given idea works or not within minutes. The catch is that the verifier can only judge finished arguments. It cannot tell you whether a half-developed idea is going anywhere. The contrast How good does a hint need to be if you can find out whether it works in five minutes? For humans, the quality bar is high because it could take months of work to pursue a hint. AI Twitter Recap Black October: AI-Accelerated Vulnerability Disclosures Overwhelm Defenders Scale of the incident wave : Over roughly 48 hours, a cluster of critical disclosures and breaches landed together ( summary , roundup , patch list ). Core software : PHP2Shell is an unauthenticated RCE in PHP. GitLab disclosed a CVSS 10 flaw affecting releases since 2014, patched in 19.5.1. Node.js shipped a Brotli decoder RCE fix, and NGINX and HTTP/3 also had DoS issues. Supply chain : LiteLLM 1.107.0 shipped with a password stealer. Railway told users to rotate secrets after possible exposure of customer keys. Zeabur is shutting down after 321,810 accounts were breached. Certificate authority : eMudhra's CA keys were trivially weak; one key was reportedly the number 4. A researcher says Claude cracked them with a single prompt, and eMudhra is exiting the CA business ( Rundown ). Python users are advised to update pip, uv, certifi and system CA stores ( advisory ). Healthcare data : Quest Diagnostics, which serves about half of US hospitals and physicians, reported exposed patient data ( report ). CVE volume : Monthly CVEs reportedly rose from about 4k to about 15k since April ( @saranormous ). State actor using agentic tooling : Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise to China-aligned Storm-0940. The group used the open agentic pentest framework ARTEX against 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants at about 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute ( MSTIC via @kimmonismus , detail ). Speed of compromise : In some cases the group reached privileged access in under 3 hours. Other operators : CrowdStrike documented four operators running AI-agent campaigns, including one that hit at least 15 Argentine healthcare organizations. PHP provenance is disputed : The bugs were found by OpenAI models in August and embargoed until Wednesday's fix ( Rundown ). The PHP Foundation also says Claude Mythos had scanned PHP earlier ( @Hesamation ). Schiff called for mandatory industry-wide AI guardrails ( post ). Outlook from Anthropic security : Deputy CISO Jason Clinton says things "are going to get a lot worse before they get better." Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
items.content: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion → The sandbox that almost didn’t make it Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch. That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat , we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion → Fast startup is an infrastructure feature Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost. We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. Jump to engineering culture → Show notes Modal — the AI infrastructure platform Erik founded. Erik’s writing — his essays on infrastructure, markets, and building companies. Modal’s Series D announcement — the company’s latest reported growth and sandbox milestones. How Modal achieved truly serverless GPUs — the startup and scaling techniques behind elastic inference. Modal’s resource solver — how it selects capacity across changing prices and availability. Scaling to one million concurrent sandboxes — an engineering account of sandbox scaling. items.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
items.content: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion → The sandbox that almost didn’t make it Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch. That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat , we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion → Fast startup is an infrastructure feature Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost. We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. items.content: Almost 2 months ago, OpenAI introduced Daybreak for Frontline Defenders , a $1B subsidy for access to Daybreak cyber models and products. That funding came into use almost immediately, as major vulnerabilities in PHP were independently discovered by two parties: Ryan Austin, a researcher at the security firm Calif, as part of the OpenAI “ Patch the Planet ” project in August 2026 using GPT 5.6 Sol: … as well as Wiz, recently acquired into Google Cloud (using Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as their own tool, Wiz Atlas). All high profile cyber disclosures are at least a little bit of marketing, and the degree to which this was a severely alarming vulnerability on the order of famous ones like log4shell and Heartbleed is up to some debate , but surely the coordinated response across the PHP Ecosystem is the developer community responding in its most ideal form. We should expect to be in for at least a year of finding such critical vulnerabilities; but it is the wrong move to blame the messenger for finding them; rather it is good to know that our critical software is generally getting the biggest security audit it has ever had in human history. AI News for 10/20/2026-10/21/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Top Story: PHP2Shell—chronology, core claims, and the complications behind the emergency response What happened Researchers disclosed two PHP-engine memory-corruption vulnerabilities, with demonstrated unauthenticated exploitation against major CMSs and an unusually broad coordinated response. The researchers named the vulnerabilities PHP2Shell and identified them as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Their technical description places the defects in PHP’s internal handling of out-of-memory conditions and fatal errors—not in a WordPress plugin or an application’s authentication logic. They report demonstrations of full remote code execution and “Heartbleed-style” memory disclosure. @sagitz_ The disclosed demonstrations included pre-authentication RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. The researcher’s announcement separately claims remote memory disclosure against any PHP application. These are researcher-reported exploit results; they should not be silently expanded into a claim that every deployment has an identical, immediately exploitable RCE path. @sagitz_ OpenAI says Calif researchers used its models to discover the flaws, while secondary reporting says Wiz independently found the same bugs. Posts identify GPT-5.6 Sol on the Calif/OpenAI side; a Wiz-affiliated account credits Gemini 4 Argon with discovery, exploit-chain development, detector creation, and patch validation. This is a multi-party discovery story, not evidence that one vendor alone found and fixed the issue. @TheRundownAI , @steipete , @ralucaadapopa OpenAI describes approximately two months of coordinated remediation before disclosure. It says the patch required a major PHP-engine change and coordination among maintainers, researchers, security providers, and governments. A participating researcher confirms work with the PHP Foundation to support and harden the patch. @OpenAI , @itszn13 Cloudflare deployed initial WAF mitigations before the scheduled patch release. Its CTO said rules covered known exploit vectors, were available to all customers including the free tier, and were being updated as early attacks emerged. He explicitly called the rules a stopgap and directed operators to patch at 14:00 UTC . @dok2001 The supplied NSA account advised preparation for an immediate update—and taking systems offline if timely mitigation was not possible. Later OpenAI messaging said upgrades were available; secondary reporting says details leaked before the patch. The supplied material does not establish precisely what leaked, when, or whether the release schedule changed. @NSACyber , @OpenAI , @TheRundownAI Reconstructing the chronology 1. Discovery and private coordination: approximately two months before public disclosure. OpenAI places the work under Patch the Planet and says it led a coalition preparing fixes and protections. Its security researcher Eric Wallace adds that internal teams worked on patching and detection rather than merely disclosing the bug, with confidential advance notification to governments and outside agencies. Greg Brockman reiterates the two-month coordination period. These are participant accounts, not an independently audited incident timeline. @Eric_Wallace_ , @gdb The distinction between program names matters: the posts associate the vulnerability with Patch the Planet , while researchers credit Daybreak model access for enabling security work. Those are related roles—remediation initiative versus access mechanism—not interchangeable descriptions of the same program. @OpenAI , @S1r1u5_ 2. Advance public warnings and a scheduled patch window. Japanese-language posts warned operators to prepare for a 23:00 JST, October 21 release, consistent with Cloudflare’s 14:00 UTC announcement. One correctly emphasized that a PHP-core vulnerability cannot be fixed merely by waiting for plugin developers. Another framed the event as a “15-minute” race after patch publication, but that number was a prediction—not a measured time to weaponization. @ds_nakajima , @expokun 3. Pre-release filtering and observed attack activity. Cloudflare’s post is the strongest firsthand operational evidence in the supplied record: mitigations were already deployed, known vectors were covered, and “early attacks” were appearing. It does not specify successful compromises, request counts, victim counts, payload provenance, or whether the traffic represented original exploit development versus reuse

items.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
items.content: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal. August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress. August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team. September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix. October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available. October 21, 2026: Public disclosure. Via Hacker News Tags: open-source , php , security , ai , ai-security-research

items.content: For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention. The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing. In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness , I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface : the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself. Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on , with models as the engine. Just as the browser became a platform for web apps, the harness could become a platform for the interfaces between people and agents. Claude Mods: What is it? A mod is a Claude Code plugin that consists of TypeScript or JavaScript functions that run inside Claude Code. These functions customize the behavior and appearance of the interface in the CLI and Desktop. Mods respond to events , like a prompt, tool call or interface render. They can observe the event, modify how it’s rendered, and handle it in place of the default behavior. Claude Mods are middleware for the agent harness . They inject code that changes Claude Code’s execution and rendering flow, changing how the application behaves at runtime. Claude Mods let the human and the agent build the human-facing part of the harness together. You can now work with Claude to design how Claude works with you. That is the essence of the “Attention Interface.” The harness reversal The agent harness started as an interface between the agent and the machine it runs on. It lets you prompt the agent and the agent then sends commands, edits files and calls tools. Now it’s gradually becoming a way for the agent to interface with the human. Claude Mods let you reverse the direction of the harness. Rather than the harness pointing from the agent to the machine, you point it from the agent to the human operator, and the harness becomes a way to interface with human attention. Claude Mods make the human layer programmable, by the human who uses Claude. Claude can also build mods for you. Claude Code has a built-in skill that teaches it how to build mods, so you can ask for the mod you want in plain language and Claude will build it. Mods in practice Some of Claude Code’s own features are already mods. Anthropic has shipped six of them built-in . You can see these by running /plugin and opening Installed , where they’re listed under Built-in: agents-md: loads AGENTS.md as project instructions. diff: takes over /diff and draws its pane. plugin-authoring: gives Claude the skill it uses to write mods for you. sec-default: guards what your organization manages from the mods a user installs. telemetry: sends the analytics records that Claude Code and its built-in mods log. you-should-know: a side agent that shows a note above the prompt when it finds something you might have missed. It’s the only one that’s off by default. Most of these work in the background, which is interesting because it means Anthropic is building parts of Claude Code as mods — even parts you may not notice. The one I’ve turned on myself is You Should Know . Here are the two mods I’ve found most useful in practice: one a built-in, and one I built myself. 1. You Should Know This is a native Claude Code plugin built by Anthropic. It runs a side-agent that observes the main agent while it works and flags important information you’re likely to miss. Think about it like: tool calls and decisions that have a material impact on the output, but aren’t necessarily easily visible because they’re buried in the agent trace. It comes built into Claude Code, but it’s off until you turn it on . Here’s a real example. I asked Claude Code to simplify the noisy UI text in one of my personal projects. The main agent trimmed the copy on the Compare screen, installed the new build and took before-and-after screenshots. Everything looked done. Then You Should Know flagged something for me. CompareView.swift, the file the agent was editing, already had uncommitted work in it — and so did about 45 other files. If I later discarded the demo edits, I’d throw away that earlier unfinished work too. Its suggestion was to commit or stash the earlier work first. In this case, the You Should Know mod saved me from discarding work unintentionally. 2. Next Steps Supervisor This mod only runs after a turn that edited files, ran commands or made 8 or more tool calls. In the screenshot below, you’ll see six different pieces of information flagged for your attention. Next Steps Supervisor then suggests a next step to take, as a clickable button which sends the instruction as a message to Claude Code. This mod is available as part of ModSmith — an open-source Claude Code plugin I built with several different built-in mods, as well as a template Claude can use to build new mods that work together.
